messages.subject: Re: Interpreting Results
messages.body_plain:
Dear Professor Royle,

Good morning. Following the code example published in "oSCR: a spatial capture–recapture R package for inference about spatial ecological processes ", I would like to ask how to compute the population size. I think is important to have an example code of how to compute the population size using oSCR.

Thanks in advance!

Victor

messages.body_plain:
hi Viktor,
 this was discussed previously in the thread:

 The intercept of the density model is log(expected number of activity centers per state-space pixel). e.g., if the result comes out to be -1 then exp(-1) = 0.368 individuals per pixel.  If the state-space is 500m x 500m then this is a density of 0.368*4 per km^2.  If you have 1000 state-space pixels then the estimated population size for the entire state-space is 368 individuals.

 So: you have to know how many pixels in your state-space in order to do this, and then N is just exp(intercept)*[Number of pixels].

regards
andy

messages.subject: RE: [oscr] Re: Interpreting Results
messages.body_plain:
HI Victor,

There are a few options here. The options in (2) give 95% CIs. Let me know if anything here doesn’t work – I’m writing this from memory.

1.      As any suggested. And you can access the number of pixels like this:

(npix <- sapply(ssDF,nrow))

And get N like this:
exp(d0)*npix

2.      The other options involVe the get.real() function:

First, compute the pixel specific densities and sum them up

pixdens <- get.real(model, type = “dens”)

apply(pixdens,2,sum)

Second, if density is constant, compute density for a single pixel and scale up using the d.factor argument

pdf <- data.frame(Session=factor(1))

get.real(model, type = “dens”, newdata = pdf, d.factor = npix)

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Victor,

Serves me right for not checking. I wasn’t sure whether you had a multisession model, but you are using the rbs data, so it has 4 sessions. I will ignore option 1 because that ran with no error. Here is the working solution for option 2, including some comments and features:

# OPTION 2A:

# Supplying no newdata object, get.real() uses the statespace object

# to compute pixel specific densities.

pixdens <- get.real(topmod, type = "dens") #takes a while

# this returns a list (length 4 = number of sessions) so

# I use the sapply function to apply the columns sums to

# each list item. Note also that I use columns 3, 5, and 6,

# these are the point estimate, and upper and lower intervals:

sapply(pixdens, function(x) apply(x[,c(3,5,6)],2,sum))

# OPTION 2B:

# Create a newdata object which has one row per session with

# a session ID column (session NOT Session <- this was the error)

pdf <- data.frame(session=factor(c(1:4)))

# Now use get.real() to compute total abundance (NB, every session

# the same number of pixels (757), this might not always be the case).

# TO get total abundance, set N_sex = FALSE:

totalpopulation <-get.real(topmod,

                           type = "dens",

                           newdata = pdf,

                           d.factor = 757,

                           N_sex=FALSE)

# Can also get sex specific estimates of N by setting N_sex = TRUE:

bysexpopulation <-get.real(topmod,

                           type = "dens",

                           newdata = pdf,

                           d.factor = 757,

                           N_sex=TRUE)

Hope that helps!

Chris

> > >  The intercept of the density model is log(expected number of activity centers per state-space pixel). e.g., if the result comes out to be -1 then exp(-1) = 0.368 individuals per pixel.  If the state-space is 500m x 500m then this is a density of 0.368*4 per km^2.  If you have 1000 state-space pixels then the estimated population size for the entire state-space is 368 individuals.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >  So: you have to know how many pixels in your state-space in order to do this, and then N is just exp(intercept)*[Number of pixels].
